commons_file: File:Don Silvestro dei Gherarducci - Nativity, in an initial P - Google Art Project.jpg
head: The first word sung at Christmas Mass, painted in gold.
sub: The big P begins Puer natus est nobis, "A child is born to us", the chant that opens the Christmas Day Mass. Florence, 1390s.
caption: This leaf comes from a giant choirbook illuminated by Don Silvestro dei Gherarducci for the abbot of San Michele a Murano. Inside the P is the Nativity. At the bottom of the page a shepherd plays the bagpipe as an angel brings the news.
credit: Don Silvestro dei Gherarducci, Nativity in an initial P, leaf from a Gradual, c. 1392 to 1399 · The Morgan Library & Museum · Public domain
audio: Gregorian chant, Introit Puer natus est nobis (unison voices)
date_why: Puer natus est is the Introit of the Christmas Day Mass.
facts_checked: c. 1392-1399, Don Silvestro dei Gherarducci for Paolo Venier, abbot of San Michele a Murano, Florence; folio 38 of the Gradual; initial P begins the Introit for Christmas Mass, Puer natus est nobis (Isaiah 9:6); shepherd plays bagpipe at bottom with angel bearing olive branch; MS M.653.1 -> https://themorgan.org/node/1192
notes: Portrait, 2456x3637. A choirbook leaf with chant notation, so it could also sit in the score row. The Virgin is nursing the Child inside the initial; small and clothed, but flagging it.

commons_file: File:Matthias Grünewald - Isenheim Altarpiece, first opening.jpg
head: An angel bows a viol for the newborn.
sub: When the Isenheim Altarpiece opens, a Concert of Angels joins the Nativity. Grünewald painted it in 1512 to 1516 for a hospital monastery.
caption: The monks of St. Anthony at Isenheim cared for the sick, and this altarpiece was made for them. In the center, a kneeling angel plays a bowed string instrument while other angels gather in a glowing chapel. To the right, Mary holds the child.
credit: Matthias Grünewald, Isenheim Altarpiece (Concert of Angels and Nativity), 1512 to 1516 · Musée Unterlinden, Colmar · Public domain
audio: Michael Praetorius, Es ist ein Ros entsprungen (viol consort)
date_why: Christmas season; Nativity with angel musicians.
facts_checked: 1512-1516, Matthias Grünewald, Unterlinden Museum Colmar; Concert of Angels and Nativity form the central scene of the opened altarpiece; painted for the Monastery of St Anthony in Issenheim, which did hospital work -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isenheim_Altarpiece
notes: MUST CROP: the full image (3200x1875) includes the Annunciation, Resurrection and the dead Christ in the predella. Crop to the two central panels (Concert of Angels and Nativity) only. Instrument described from the image.

commons_file: File:Dante Gabriel Rossetti - A Christmas Carol.jpg
head: Rossetti's Christmas carol, sung in gold and holly.
sub: In 1867 Rossetti painted Ellen Smith singing a carol to an old tune and plucking a stringed instrument topped with a sprig of holly.
caption: Rossetti fixed a short text to the frame describing a richly dressed maid singing of Christ's birth to an old carol melody. Look at the holly berries tied to the head of the instrument and her fingers on the strings. It was his second picture with this title, after a watercolor of 1857 to 1858.
credit: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, A Christmas Carol, 1867 · Private collection · Public domain
audio: Traditional English, The Holly and the Ivy (solo piano)
date_why: Christmas week; the painting is titled A Christmas Carol.
facts_checked: 1867, oil, model Ellen Smith, owner The Viscount Leverhulme; second picture with this title, first a watercolour 1857-58; legend on frame describes a maid singing a Christmas song to an old carol tune -> https://rossettiarchive.iath.virginia.edu/docs/s195.rap.html
notes: Portrait, 1668x2000. Credit says 'Private collection' (Rossetti Archive lists The Viscount Leverhulme). Instrument and holly read from the image.

commons_file: File:Johann Strauss II at the Court Ball by Theo Zasche.jpg
head: The Waltz King conducts a Vienna court ball.
sub: Johann Strauss II led up to 40 musicians at the imperial court balls. Theo Zasche drew the scene around 1890, violin bow in Strauss's hand.
caption: Until 1870, Strauss played the annual court balls, family balls and children's balls of the Habsburg court. For family balls in the imperial apartments, the band shrank to about ten players. Look for Strauss at the front, leading with his violin.
credit: Theo Zasche, Johann Strauss II and his orchestra at a court ball, c. 1890 · Wien Museum · Public domain
audio: Johann Strauss II, Kaiser-Walzer (Emperor Waltz), Op. 437 (piano)
date_why: New Year's Day, the day of Vienna's Strauss-filled New Year's Concert.
facts_checked: Up to 40 musicians at court balls, about ten at family balls in imperial apartments; until 1870 Strauss played annual court balls, family and children's balls; coloured print after a watercolour by Theodor Zasche, c. 1890, Wien Museum -> https://habsburger.net/en/media/johann-strauss-his-orchestra-court-ball-coloured-print-after-watercolour-theodor-zasche-c
notes: Landscape, 3518x2778. Commons dates the file 1888; habsburger.net (Wien Museum) says c. 1890 (used). 'Violin bow in his hand' read from the image, please confirm. Zasche died 1922.

commons_file: File:1899 poster of Mme. M. Sissieretta Jones.jpg
head: Madame Jones, and every medal she was given.
sub: Sissieretta Jones sang for four presidents, starting with Benjamin Harrison in 1892, and was the first African American to sing at what became Carnegie Hall.
caption: A critic nicknamed her the Black Patti, after the opera star Adelina Patti; she preferred Madame Jones. In 1892 she sang for about 75,000 people at Madison Square Garden. This 1899 poster shows her wearing her medals.
credit: Poster for Mme. M. Sissieretta Jones, The Black Patti, 1899 · Library of Congress · Public domain
audio: Giuseppe Verdi, Addio del passato from La traviata (voice and piano)
date_why: Sissieretta Jones was born January 5, 1868 or 1869.
facts_checked: Born January 5, 1868 or 1869, Portsmouth, Virginia; 'Black Patti' given by a New York Clipper critic, she preferred Madame Jones; sang for Benjamin Harrison (Feb 1892), Cleveland, McKinley, T. Roosevelt; about 75,000 at Madison Square Garden April 1892, sang La traviata selections; first African American to sing at the Music Hall, renamed Carnegie Hall -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sissieretta_Jones
notes: Portrait, 7728x11848 (huge). Poster tagline at bottom uses period wording ('of her race'); consider cropping to the portrait and medals. Audio: she sang La traviata selections in 1892; the specific aria is a fit, not a documented performance.

commons_file: File:Monsieur de Saint-George Ward Brown Angelo Meyer Gallica-color.jpg
head: Violinist, composer, conductor and champion fencer.
sub: Joseph Bologne, Chevalier de Saint-Georges, born in Guadeloupe on Christmas Day 1745, led the Paris orchestra that premiered Haydn's Paris symphonies.
caption: Saint-Georges was the son of a planter and Nanon, an enslaved woman. In Paris he beat the best swordsmen of his day, led the Concert des Amateurs and wrote some of the first string quartets in France. This 1788 engraving copies a portrait that hung in Henry Angelo's fencing academy in London.
credit: William Ward after Mather Brown, Monsieur de St. George, 1788 · Bibliothèque nationale de France · Public domain
audio: Joseph Bologne, Chevalier de Saint-Georges, String Quartet Op. 1 No. 1 (string quartet)
facts_checked: Born 25 December 1745, Baillif, Guadeloupe; mother Nanon, enslaved; father a planter; beat best swordsmen; concertmaster then conductor of Concert des Amateurs; in 1785 conducted premieres of Haydn's Paris symphonies with the Loge Olympique; Op. 1 quartets c. 1770-71 among first in France; Mather Brown portrait given to Henry Angelo -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bologne,_Chevalier_de_Saint-Georges

Engraving by William Ward after Mather Brown 'from an Original Picture at Mr Angelo's Fencing Academy', 1788 -> https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monsieur_de_Saint-George_Ward_Brown_Angelo_Meyer_Gallica-color.jpg
notes: Portrait, 4266x5536. He led the Loge Olympique orchestra for the Haydn premieres (sub says 'the Paris orchestra'). 'London' for Angelo's academy is general knowledge; Wikipedia says he sat for Brown in England.

head: The London composer welcomed at the White House.
sub: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor's Hiawatha's Wedding Feast (1898) made him famous. On his first US tour in 1904, Theodore Roosevelt received him.
caption: In Washington, D.C., a 200-voice African American chorus named itself the Samuel Coleridge-Taylor Society in 1901. He toured the United States three times, in 1904, 1906 and 1910. He died in 1912, aged just 37.
credit: Photographer unknown, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, c. 1905 · Public domain
audio: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, Twenty-Four Negro Melodies, Op. 59 (1905), a selection (piano solo)
facts_checked: Born 15 August 1875 London, died 1 September 1912; Hiawatha's Wedding Feast premiered 1898; US tours 1904, 1906, 1910; received by Theodore Roosevelt at the White House on 1904 tour; Samuel Coleridge-Taylor Society, 200-voice chorus, founded in Washington 1901; Op. 59 dated 1905 -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Coleridge-Taylor
notes: Portrait, 2460x3712 (restored scan). Holding collection not stated on Commons; credit leaves it out. Op. 59 title is the 1905 published title; curator may prefer to name one piece.

head: The choir that sang a university into being.
sub: The Fisk Jubilee Singers set out on October 6, 1871, to raise money for Fisk University. Their tours paid for its first permanent building, Jubilee Hall.
caption: In 1873 the group sang "Steal Away to Jesus" and "Go Down, Moses" for Queen Victoria. This group portrait was printed as the frontispiece of a book in the 1870s. Among the faces are Ella Sheppard, Maggie Porter and Thomas Rutling.
credit: Anonymous, Group Portrait of the Jubilee Singers (Woodburytype), 1872 to 1877 · Rijksmuseum · CC0
audio: Traditional spiritual, Steal Away to Jesus (vocal ensemble)
facts_checked: Founded 1871 to raise money for Fisk; first tour October 6, 1871, under George L. White; European tour money paid for Jubilee Hall, Fisk's first permanent building; sang 'Steal Away to Jesus' and 'Go Down, Moses' for Queen Victoria in April 1873 -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisk_Jubilee_Singers

Woodburytype, 1872 to in or before 1877, print opposite title page; sitters incl. Maggie Porter, Thomas Rutling, Ella Sheppard -> https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jubilee_Singers,_RP-F-F25357.jpg
notes: Portrait, 4512x5644, CC0. Small original print, so expect softness at full zoom. The Rijksmuseum lists ten sitters; caption names three.

head: He heard a piece once and could play it back.
sub: Thomas Wiggins, born enslaved and blind in Georgia in 1849, was said to know 7,000 pieces. In 1860 he played for President Buchanan at the White House.
caption: Promoters toured him from the age of eight, sometimes four shows a day, and the family that held him kept most of what he earned. He was also a composer of piano pieces. This photograph shows him around 1880.
credit: Blind Tom (Thomas Wiggins), c. 1880 · Library of Congress · Public domain
audio: Thomas Wiggins, Water in the Moonlight (piano solo)
facts_checked: Born May 25, 1849, Georgia plantation, blind from birth; sold with his parents to James Neil Bethune; reportedly learned 7,000 pieces, often after one hearing; 1860 performed for President Buchanan, first African American command performance there; hired out at eight to promoter Perry Oliver, sometimes four shows a day; Bethune family reportedly earned about $750,000 -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Tom_Wiggins
notes: Portrait, 1169x1536. Date c. 1880 from the Commons/LoC record. Audio: please confirm 'Water in the Moonlight' is a Wiggins piece before use (not checked); fallback is any Wiggins piano piece. Avoid his Battle of Manassas (it celebrates a Confederate victory).

commons_file: File:Johann Strauss II by Hans Schliessmann.jpg
head: The Blue Danube was first sung, not danced.
sub: Strauss's Op. 314 premiered on February 15, 1867, as a piece for men's chorus, sung by the Vienna Men's Choral Association at the Dianabad.
caption: The orchestral version came later and conquered the world. Viennese artist Hans Schließmann, known for his portraits of musicians, caught Strauss in silhouette. Watch the posture: violin up, all motion.
credit: Hans Schließmann, Johann Strauss II (silhouette), before 1920 · Public domain
audio: Johann Strauss II, An der schönen blauen Donau, Op. 314 (piano solo)
facts_checked: Premiere 15 February 1867 at the Diana Baths (Dianabad), Vienna, conducted by Rudolf Weinwurm, at a concert of the Wiener Männergesang-Verein, words by Joseph Weyl; Op. 314 -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blue_Danube
Hans Schließmann, born 1852 Mainz, died 1920 Vienna, known for portraits of musicians -> https://austria-forum.org/af/AEIOU/Schlie%C3%9Fmann%2C_Hans/Schlie%C3%9Fmann%2C_Hans_english
notes: Portrait, 2230x2460. Detail of a book cover ('Dirigenten'); Commons gives no date beyond the artist's death in 1920. 'Violin up' read from the image, please confirm. 'Conquered the world' is a loose phrase; curator may tone down. Black silhouette on light ground.

head: The first woman to win the Prix de Rome, baton in hand.
sub: In 1913 Lili Boulanger, 19, won first prize with her cantata Faust et Hélène. Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret sketched her conducting it.
caption: The Prix de Rome was France's top prize for young composers, and no woman had won it before. Boulanger died in 1918 at only 24. Her piano piece D'un jardin clair dates from 1914.
credit: Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret, Lili Boulanger conducting her cantata Faust et Hélène, 1913 · Public domain
audio: Lili Boulanger, D'un jardin clair (piano solo)
facts_checked: Born 21 August 1893, died 15 March 1918 aged 24; won the 1913 Prix de Rome with Faust et Hélène, first woman to win first prize; D'un jardin clair, 1914, solo piano -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lili_Boulanger
Sketch by Dagnan-Bouveret of Boulanger conducting her cantata -> https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lili-Boulanger-dirigeant-sa-cantate-Dagnan-Bouveret.jpg
notes: Portrait, 1582x2530. Holding collection not given on Commons. 'France's top prize for young composers' is general; acceptable but unsourced. Age 19 at the 1913 prize (born Aug 1893, prize July 1913).

commons_file: File:Elisabeth Claude Jacquet de La Guerre - L. Crepy sculp. - btv1b8421266c.jpg
head: She played for Louis XIV at five. Then she wrote an opera.
sub: Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre's Céphale et Procris, 1694, was the first opera by a woman staged in France. Her harpsichord book came out in 1687.
caption: As a child she performed at Versailles and caught the king's eye. Her 1687 Pièces de clavecin was one of the few harpsichord books printed in France in that century. A writer of the time placed her on his French Parnassus beside Marais and Lalande, praising her improvised preludes.
credit: Louis Crépy, Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre (engraved portrait), 1729 · Bibliothèque nationale de France · Public domain
audio: Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre, Suite in D minor from Pièces de clavecin, 1687 (harpsichord)
facts_checked: Born 17 March 1665, died 27 June 1729; performed at Versailles at five, noticed by Louis XIV; Pièces de clavessin 1687, one of few printed in France in 17th c.; Céphale et Procris 15 March 1694; Titon du Tillet placed her on his Parnassus next to Lalande and Marais, praised preludes off the cuff -> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89lisabeth_Jacquet_de_La_Guerre
notes: Very tall (1944x4536); likely includes a long text panel below the portrait; crop to the portrait. Date 1729 from BnF/Commons. 'First opera by a woman staged in France' is the usual claim; Wikipedia gives premiere 1694 at the Académie Royale. The 1687 book includes a D minor suite (not checked); curator may simplify audio to 'Pièces de clavecin (1687)'. Her birthday (March 17) falls outside the window.
